When you hear that a medicine has been “approved,” what does that actually mean? In short, a regulator has looked at the evidence from clinical trials and decided that the benefits outweigh the risks for a particular group of people. It doesn’t mean the drug is perfectly safe — all medicines have side effects — or that it works for everyone. Approval comes with a label that lists the uses, the right dose, and the warnings you should know about. After a drug hits the market, the agency keeps watching for problems, collecting reports from doctors and patients. If you think you’ve had a bad reaction to something, you can report it yourself. And as always, talk with your pharmacist or doctor if you have questions.
